source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN Examination, 7th ed.

questions.subject: NP V
questions.stem: A client is started on amitriptyline for depression. Which common side effect should the nurse monitor for?
questions.rationale: Tricyclic antidepressants commonly cause drowsiness, fatigue, and sedation, along with anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation) and hypotension.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q341 (PDF p. 509)
questions.quote: Common side effects of amitriptyline (a tricyclic antidepressant) include the central nervous system effects of drowsiness, fatigue, lethargy, and sedation.

questions.subject: NP II
questions.topic: Care of Mother During Labor and Birth
questions.stem: Which statement by a mother shows she understands why her newborn needs a vitamin K (phytonadione) injection?
options: 'The baby's liver cannot make vitamin K at all.'
'Newborns lack the gut bacteria that make vitamin K.'
questions.rationale: The newborn gut lacks the normal flora that synthesize vitamin K, causing a temporary clotting deficiency in the first days of life. The injection prevents bleeding.
explanations: The liver uses vitamin K; the problem is the lack of gut flora.
Correct: there are no intestinal bacteria yet to produce vitamin K.
Vitamin K prevents bleeding, not jaundice.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q344 (PDF p. 512)
questions.quote: The absence of normal flora needed to synthesize vitamin K (phytonadione) in the normal newborn gut results in low levels of vitamin K

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Aspirin is given to a client before percutaneous transluminal coronary angioplasty (PTCA). What is its purpose?
options: To relieve pain after the procedure
To prevent fever after the procedure
questions.rationale: Aspirin inhibits platelet aggregation, reducing the risk of the artery occluding during and after angioplasty.
explanations: Not the reason for giving it before PTCA.
Correct: it is an antiplatelet agent.
Aspirin does not lower blood pressure.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q347 (PDF p. 515)
questions.quote: the aspirin inhibits platelet aggregation.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Acetaminophen is prescribed to be given before a topical nitrate. What is the reason?
options: Headache is a common side effect of nitrates
It prevents fever caused by the nitrate
It protects the stomach from the nitrate
questions.rationale: Nitrates dilate blood vessels, which often causes headache. Acetaminophen given beforehand prevents or lessens it. The headaches usually lessen with continued use.
explanations: It does not potentiate the nitrate.
Topical nitrates do not irritate the stomach.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q348 (PDF p. 516)
questions.quote: Headache occurs as a side effect of nitrates in many clients.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.situation: Mang Ernesto, 68, has atrial fibrillation and is discharged on warfarin to prevent stroke.
questions.stem: Which food should Mang Ernesto limit because of its high vitamin K content?
questions.rationale: Warfarin works against vitamin K-dependent clotting factors, so intake of vitamin K-rich foods (green leafy vegetables, broccoli, cabbage, turnips, liver, tea) is kept limited and consistent.
explanations: Oranges are high in vitamin C, not K.
Correct: broccoli is high in vitamin K.
Strawberries are high in vitamin C.
Rice is low in vitamin K.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q350 (PDF p. 518)
questions.quote: These foods include coffee or tea (caffeine), turnips, cabbage, broccoli, greens, fish, and liver.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.situation: Mang Ernesto, 68, has atrial fibrillation and is discharged on warfarin to prevent stroke.
questions.stem: The nurse tells Mang Ernesto to shave with an electric razor. Which reason BEST supports this instruction?
options: Cuts and bleeding must be avoided
Blades contain metals that react with warfarin
questions.rationale: Anticoagulants increase the risk of bleeding, so clients are taught measures that prevent cuts, such as using an electric razor and a soft toothbrush.
explanations: Correct: the goal is to prevent bleeding.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q473 (PDF p. 657)
questions.quote: The importance of use of an electric razor is to prevent cuts and possible bleeding.

questions.subject: NP I
questions.topic: Care of Individuals: Communicable & Non-Communicable Diseases
questions.stem: A client starting TB treatment under DOTS is prescribed rifampin. Which side effect should the nurse tell the client to expect?
questions.rationale: Rifampin turns urine, sweat, and tears orange; soft contact lenses can be permanently stained. Rifampin is hepatotoxic, so yellow sclera would be a warning sign, not an expected effect.
explanations: Jaundice suggests hepatotoxicity and must be reported.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q353 (PDF p. 521)
questions.quote: Secretions will become orange in color as a result of the rifampin.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A client receiving cisplatin complains of ringing in the ears. The nurse recognizes this as:
options: An expected sign that the drug is working
An allergic reaction to the infusion
questions.rationale: Cisplatin, a platinum compound, can cause ototoxicity with tinnitus and hearing loss. The nurse assesses hearing during therapy.
explanations: Tinnitus is a toxic effect, not a sign of effectiveness.
Not the cause of tinnitus here.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q366 (PDF p. 534)
questions.quote: An adverse effect related to the administration of cisplatin is ototoxicity with hearing loss.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.situation: Mrs. Garcia, 55, has type 1 diabetes and is admitted for blood sugar control. She receives 8 units of regular insulin subcutaneously at 7:30 AM.
questions.stem: At what time should the nurse be MOST alert for hypoglycemia?
questions.rationale: Regular insulin starts working in about 30 minutes, peaks in 2 to 4 hours, and lasts 4 to 6 hours. Hypoglycemia is most likely at the peak: 9:30 to 11:30 AM.
explanations: Correct: 2 to 4 hours after the dose.
Near the end of its duration.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q370 (PDF p. 538)
questions.quote: Its onset of action occurs in a half hour and peaks in 2 to 4 hours.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.situation: Mrs. Garcia, 55, has type 1 diabetes and is admitted for blood sugar control. She receives 8 units of regular insulin subcutaneously at 7:30 AM.
questions.stem: Mrs. Garcia's blood glucose is 62 mg/dL. Which finding does the nurse expect?
questions.rationale: Hypoglycemia (below 70 mg/dL) causes hunger, sweating, weakness, nervousness, cool clammy skin, blurred vision, tachycardia, and palpitations. Polyuria is a sign of hyperglycemia.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q381 (PDF p. 550)
questions.quote: Clinical manifestations of hypoglycemia include hunger, sweating, weakness, nervousness, cool clammy skin

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A client received atropine sulfate before surgery. Which effect should the nurse monitor for in the immediate postoperative period?
questions.rationale: Atropine is an anticholinergic. It causes tachycardia, drowsiness, blurred vision, dry mouth, constipation, and urinary retention. It is contraindicated in glaucoma.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q377 (PDF p. 546)
questions.quote: Atropine sulfate is an anticholinergic medication that causes tachycardia, drowsiness, blurred vision, dry mouth, constipation, and urinary retention.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Flecainide is prescribed for a client with frequent runs of ventricular tachycardia. Which safety measure is MOST specific to this drug?
options: Monitoring for new or worsening dysrhythmias
Checking the blood glucose before meals
questions.rationale: Flecainide slows conduction and reduces excitability, but it can itself cause new or worse dysrhythmias (proarrhythmia). Cardiac rhythm monitoring is the key safety measure.
explanations: Standard care, not specific to flecainide.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q399 (PDF p. 569)
questions.quote: the nurse must monitor for the development of a new or worsening dysrhythmia.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: A client is prescribed valproic acid 250 mg once daily for seizures. When is the SAFEST time to give it?
questions.rationale: Valproic acid depresses the CNS, causing sedation, dizziness, ataxia, and confusion. A single daily dose at bedtime reduces the risk of injury; a snack lessens GI upset.
explanations: Daytime sedation increases the risk of falls.
Daytime sedation increases the risk of falls.
Daytime sedation increases the risk of falls.
Correct: bedtime dosing reduces injury risk.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q406 (PDF p. 580)
questions.quote: administering it at bedtime negates the risk of injury from sedation and enhances client safety.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Just before an IV dose of tobramycin, the client reports dizziness and ringing in the ears. What should the nurse do?
options: Give an antiemetic with the dose
Hold the dose and notify the physician
questions.rationale: Vertigo and tinnitus suggest eighth cranial nerve damage (ototoxicity), which can become permanent hearing loss. The dose is held and the prescriber notified.
explanations: Giving the dose risks permanent hearing loss.
Treating the symptom ignores the toxicity.
Correct: hold the dose and report it.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q429 (PDF p. 607)
questions.quote: Ringing in the ears and vertigo are two symptoms that may indicate dysfunction of the eighth cranial nerve.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Which safety measure must be in place before giving IV amiodarone for a life-threatening ventricular dysrhythmia?
questions.rationale: Amiodarone treats life-threatening ventricular dysrhythmias. The client must be on continuous cardiac monitoring, and the drug is given by infusion pump.
explanations: May be in place but is not specific to amiodarone.
Oximetry alone does not monitor rhythm.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q430 (PDF p. 608)
questions.quote: The client should have continuous cardiac monitoring in place for safety

questions.subject: NP V
questions.stem: The nurse is about to inject IV hydralazine for a client in hypertensive crisis. Which item must be in place?
options: A blood pressure cuff at the bedside
A cooling blanket on the bed
questions.rationale: Hydralazine lowers blood pressure quickly, so BP and pulse are monitored frequently after it is given. A peripheral IV is enough.
explanations: A central line is not necessary.
Correct: frequent BP monitoring is required.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q436 (PDF p. 614)
questions.quote: The blood pressure and pulse should be monitored frequently after administration

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: A client's clonazepam dose for a seizure disorder is being adjusted. Which nursing measure is the PRIORITY?
questions.rationale: During initial therapy and dose adjustments of an anticonvulsant, seizure control can change, so seizure precautions are instituted. Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines.
explanations: Correct: seizure risk changes during adjustment.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q440 (PDF p. 620)
questions.quote: During initial therapy and periods of dosage adjustment, the nurse should initiate seizure precautions for the client.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: Before giving oral pyridostigmine to a client with myasthenia gravis, what should the nurse check FIRST?
options: The ability to swallow, using sips of water
The time of the last bowel movement
questions.rationale: Myasthenia gravis can weaken the swallowing muscles. The first assessment is whether the client can safely take oral medications, such as by trying sips of water.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q447 (PDF p. 627)
questions.quote: The primary assessment is to determine the client’s ability to handle oral medications or any oral substance.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: A client has taken metoclopramide for a long time. Which finding should the nurse report to the physician IMMEDIATELY?
questions.rationale: Uncontrolled rhythmic movements of the face or limbs suggest tardive dyskinesia, which may be irreversible. The drug is stopped and the prescriber notified.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q451 (PDF p. 631)
questions.quote: If the client experiences tardive dyskinesia (rhythmic movements of the face or limbs), the nurse should call the primary health care provider

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A client on a heparin infusion after a myocardial infarction has an aPTT of 100 seconds. Before reporting it, which drug should the nurse make sure is available?
questions.rationale: An aPTT of 100 seconds exceeds the therapeutic range (about 60 to 70 seconds) and means a risk of bleeding. Protamine sulfate is the antidote for heparin.
explanations: FFP is used for warfarin-related bleeding.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q590 (PDF p. 798)
questions.quote: The antidote for heparin overdosage is protamine sulfate and may be prescribed.

questions.subject: NP II
questions.stem: Methylergonovine is prescribed for a postpartum client. Which finding should make the nurse verify the order with the physician?
options: Continuous trickle of bright red blood
questions.rationale: Methylergonovine treats uterine atony but is contraindicated in hypertension. Heavy lochia and a boggy fundus are the very signs it treats.
explanations: A sign of atony that the drug treats.
A sign of atony that the drug treats.
Bleeding from atony is an indication for the drug.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q505 (PDF p. 700)
questions.quote: It is contraindicated for the hypertensive woman, individuals with severe hepatic or renal disease, and during the third stage of labor.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Which instruction should the nurse give a postoperative client using a patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) pump?
options: 'Push the button before the pain becomes severe.'
'Ask your family to press it while you sleep.'
'Wait until the pain is unbearable to press it.'
'Press it every few minutes even without pain.'
questions.rationale: The client presses the button before pain becomes too great and reports nausea, vomiting, inability to void, and breakthrough pain. Only the client should press the button.
explanations: Correct: early dosing keeps pain under control.
Others pressing the button risks overdose.
Severe pain is harder to control.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q515 (PDF p. 710)
questions.quote: The client needs to be instructed to push the button before the pain becomes too great.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: IV foscarnet is prescribed for CMV retinitis in a client with AIDS. What should the nurse do before giving it?
options: Prepare folic acid as an antidote
Run it on a controlled infusion device
Give it as a rapid IV push
questions.rationale: Foscarnet is potentially toxic, especially to the kidneys, so it is given with a controlled infusion device and serum creatinine is checked often.
explanations: Folic acid is not an antidote for foscarnet.
Correct: controlled infusion for a toxic drug.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q548 (PDF p. 749)
questions.quote: Because of the potential toxicity of the medication, it is administered with the use of a controlled infusion device.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: A client with Parkinson's disease recently started on levodopa is about to walk. What is MOST important to assess first?
questions.rationale: Parkinson's disease causes orthostatic hypotension, and levodopa makes it worse. Checking postural vital signs before walking the client prevents falls.
explanations: Helpful, but not the most important here.
Helpful, but not the most important here.
Correct: levodopa adds to orthostatic hypotension.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q592 (PDF p. 800)
questions.quote: This problem is exacerbated with the introduction of levodopa, which can also cause postural hypotension.
